suggestions.title: Global organic chemicals industry under the CBAM: Changes in output, carbon emissions and cross-country inequality
suggestions.authors: Chenchen Wang, Laijun Zhao, Juntao Zhen, George N Papageorgiou
suggestions.abstract: The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is poised to potentially cover the organic‑chemical industry after 2026, carrying far‑reaching consequences for global production, emissions and international fairness. This study assesses CBAM impacts across 42 major economies by combining an input‑output‑based emission intensity approach, a Two‑Stage Armington partial‑equilibrium model, and a sector‑level weighted inequality index. Simulations are implemented under a no‑CBAM baseline and a counterfactual CBAM policy setting, with two further emissions‑accounting scenarios: direct‑emission‑only (Scenario 1), and direct plus electricity‑related indirect emissions (Scenario 2). Going beyond prior work focused largely on output and emission shifts, this paper incorporates cross‑country inequality metrics to unpack policy distributional consequences. Results show that CBAM expands domestic output within the EU while contracting output in non‑EU regions, with larger effects under Scenario 2. All EU sub‑regions, particularly Western Europe, experience rising carbon emissions, whereas most non‑EU regions see emission reductions. CBAM widens cross‑country inequality, more sharply outside than inside the EU; the greatest inequality occurs in Central and Eastern Europe, as well as Russia, the Middle East and Norway. These findings expose sector‑level asymmetric and distributional harms of CBAM and offer empirical evidence for global chemical decarbonization, climate‑policy

suggestions.title: Carbon Prices and Cooking Fires: How Decarbonization Pathway Design Shapes Household Energy Burdens
suggestions.authors: Mel George, Leon Clarke, Jihoon Min et al.
suggestions.abstract: Pathways reaching the same climate target can distribute household energy costs very differently across income groups. We compare 16 core mitigation pathways spanning a cost-optimal benchmark and technology, timing, effort-sharing, and demand-side designs, plus one rebound sensitivity, within a common integrated assessment framework. All core pathways remain below 2°C and converge to approximately 1.5°C warming by 2100, consistent with the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C temperature goal. We translate energy- and food-price outcomes into household energy burdens across income deciles in India and the United States using survey-informed downscaling. In 2030, cost-optimal, technology, and pace pathways are regressive in both countries, with larger burden increases for poorer deciles. In India, lower-demand pathways reduce global carbon prices and lower burdens for poorer households, whereas accelerated electrification and rapid traditional-biomass phase-out raise burdens. Historical-responsibility transfers lower burdens in India and raise them in the United States under the stylized transfer design. A conventional gross-income sensitivity preserves pathway rankings and almost all decile-level burden-change signs but roughly halves poorest-decile magnitudes in India. Accounting for food expenditure therefore reveals affordability pressures on poorer households that gross-income measures mute. Scenario design is an equity-relevant dimension of pathway assessment alongside revenue recycl

suggestions.title: Assessing processes and evidence for Highest Possible Ambition in Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement
suggestions.authors: Julia K Schönfeld, Setu Pelz, Hamish Beath, Joeri Rogelj
suggestions.abstract: The Paris Agreement establishes that Parties’ Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) will represent a progression, a country’s Highest Possible Ambition (HPA), and an equitable contribution to the collective long-term temperature goal. However, the Agreement provides no guidance on how the HPA standard should be interpreted, assessed, or operationalised in practice. In response to this gap, initial scholarship has proposed frameworks to interpret HPA based on the treaty's text and the wider international environmental law context, which includes the 2025 Advisory Opinion on Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change from the International Court of Justice. Altogether, this has clarified how HPA is part of states’ due diligence obligations and sets the stage for the next challenge: how can the theoretical understanding of HPA be practically applied to assess whether NDCs reflect this norm? Here, we build on existing reporting obligations under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), emerging approaches reflected in the UNFCCC NDC synthesis report, and best practices from the research community. We describe expectations for the process, conduct, presentation, and documentation of NDCs of highest possible ambition. suggestions.title: Nearly ninety percent of Indonesian coffee area is classified as deforestation-free under the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)
suggestions.authors: Tin Widyani Satriawan, Xiangzhong (Remi) Luo, Shafira N Ramdhania et al.
suggestions.abstract: Indonesia is the third-largest coffee producer globally and exports a substantial share of its production to European Union (EU) countries. Recent implementation of the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which requires deforestation-free supply chains, highlights the need for spatially-explicit coffee mapping to support the assessment of coffee-associated deforestation. In this study, we utilized multitemporal and multi-sensor remote sensing to produce annual maps of coffee distribution from 2016 to 2024. We analyzed the spatial patterns of annual coffee distribution during this period, and evaluated the potential implications of EUDR for coffee production in Indonesia. Our maps of coffee agroecosystems demonstrate an overall classification accuracy exceeding 80%, and are broadly consistent with independent coffee datasets (i.e., national statistics and coffee probability maps from the Forest Data Partnership). We detected a net increase of ~15% in coffee area over the eight-year period, although the patterns of change vary across provinces. Based on these maps, we estimate that 87.9% of the coffee area in 2024 meets the EUDR deforestation-free criterion, and only a relatively small proportion of agroecosystems are classified as non-deforestation-free. suggestions.title: Dynamic urban decarbonisation pathways revealed in rapidly urbanizing Chinese cities
suggestions.authors: Tong Chen, Felix Creutzig, Ramit Debnath
suggestions.abstract: Urban economies and their associated $CO_2$ emissions depend on a specific urban structure and change dynamically. However, few studies have captured the co-evolution of carbon and broader urban development, or identified the governance-related factors associated with such change across different types of cities. This study addresses this gap by analysing data from 232 Chinese cities between 1999 and 2019. As a key novel contribution, we investigate urban types as dynamic states {by applying K-Means++ clustering to pooled city-year observations,} and identify six archetypes of urban carbon evolution, together with three typical transition pathways. We further apply a Low Carbon City indicator framework and develop a pooled CatBoost model selected from five candidate algorithms, using SHAP values to interpret archetype-stratified feature contributions to carbon emission predictions. Our identified pathways indicate that carbon control can be compatible with rapid economic development. Cities with similar per capita emissions can nevertheless differ in transition maturity, highlighting distinct capacities and priorities for further decarbonisation. suggestions.title: Lithium Constraints on India’s Transport Electrification: System-Level Impacts and Policy Implications for the Net-Zero Transition
suggestions.authors: Anu Agarwal, Amit Kanudia, Tarun Sharma
suggestions.abstract: Energy transition pathways have largely treated critical minerals as unconstrained for the deployment of low-carbon energy technologies. This paper challenges this assumption for India, the third-largest energy consumer globally and a major importer of battery-grade minerals, by incorporating lithium supply limitations within an integrated energy-system framework and quantifying the consequences on technology choices, electrification, and transition costs. This study assesses the feasibility of decarbonization pathways using the long-term energy-system models from a critical minerals availability constraints perspective. Using the KINESYS-TIMES model, seventeen scenarios combine three lithium-intensity sensitivities (kg of lithium per kWh of installed battery capacity) with four availability cases (30%, 60% and 90% of unconstrained net-zero requirements, and unconstrained), two dynamic recycling variants, and three runs under an Accelerated Policies scenario of intermediate ambition. The availability is enforced within the optimization; hence the substitutability comes from cost minimization, not from post hoc accounting, and the marginal value of the constraint becomes apparent. Lithium retained in the operational fleet grows twentyfold between 2030 and 2070 from 36.8 to 728.4 kt/yr with post-2040 being the risk period. suggestions.title: Beyond 2030: what sectoral shifts in EU and China reveal about Long Term climate commitments
suggestions.authors: Eleftheria Zisarou, Panagiotis Fragkos, Dirk-Jan van de Ven, Songmin Yu
suggestions.abstract: The European Union (EU) and China, as two of the largest economies and emitters, play a pivotal role in the global energy transition. While both economies have committed to ambitious decarbonization pledges in the form of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and Long-Term Targets (LTTs) under the Paris Agreement, the feasibility of their mid-century climate goals remains uncertain. This work employs two leading Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs)—PROMETHEUS and GCAM—to compare the sectoral emissions reductions, final-energy mix, electrification rates and technology mixes associated with NDC–LTT-consistent pathways in the two regions. The study uses a scenario based on the combination of NDCs and LTTs to identify post-2030 sectoral shifts across major economic and emitting sectors. The findings show that China relies on concentrated post-2030 power and industrial decarbonisation, while the EU pathway depends more on sustained fossilfuel exit in end-use sectors. These contrasts point to different implementation risks: China needs early preparation for a compressed post-2030 power–industry transition, whereas the EU needs stronger delivery in residual fossil-fuel use across buildings, transport and industrial heat. By distinguishing robust requirements from model dependent uncertainties, the analysis identifies where future NDCs should move from aggregate pledges to sector-specific roadmaps backed by policy instruments, investment strategies and implementation capacity

suggestions.title: Beyond efficiency: Disentangling structural and behavioral sufficiency in U.S. residential decarbonization pathways
suggestions.authors: Shuhaib Nawawi, Parth Vaishnav, Xiaoyang Zhong et al.
suggestions.abstract: Decarbonization strategies in the residential sector have largely focused on lowering the carbon intensity of energy supply and improving end-use efficiency. Sufficiency, defined as avoiding unnecessary energy demand while maintaining well-being, remains largely absent from national energy system analyses, obscuring the relative and combined roles of efficiency and sufficiency in reducing energy demand. Here, we disentangle the effects of structural and behavioral sufficiency on residential energy demand and emissions, and quantify their individual and combined effects alongside efficiency improvements and heating electrification. Using an integrated modeling framework that links U.S. housing stock turnover to hourly building energy demand, we find that floorspace expands by 55% from 2020 to 2050 under business-as-usual trends, increasing energy demand by 8%. Relative to this 2050 trajectory, efficiency and structural sufficiency reduce demand by 26% and 24%, and by 44% when combined. Adopting conservative, health-informed thermostat setpoints further reduces energy demand by 29–44%. These results show that accounting for sufficiency changes the scale of residential energy demand reductions achievable under decarbonization pathways, highlighting the importance of how buildings are used alongside what is built in bringing the sector closer to deep decarbonization while maintaining household well-being.

suggestions.title: The impact of financing cost differences on global energy and industry decarbonization
suggestions.authors: Paul Waidelich, Constance Crassier, Harmen Sytze de Boer et al.
suggestions.abstract: Integrated assessment models usually neglect differences in financing conditions across countries, sectors and time. This omission could distort outcomes concerning electricity generation and also other sectors. Here we estimate and implement dynamic, country-specific cost of capital (CoC) for eight energy and industry sectors in the IMAGE integrated assessment model. Compared with assuming a uniform low-risk CoC, accounting for developing countries’ investment risks increases global mitigation costs through 2100 for staying well below +2 °C by around 9% and shifts cost-effective mitigation efforts to lower-risk regions. Sector-level analysis shows that using granular CoC estimates reduces grid investments in developing countries, shifts centralized heat production towards natural gas and raises green hydrogen costs, slowing electrolysis uptake. In industries such as steel and cement, sector and country risks hinder capital-intensive carbon capture and electricity-based technologies. Our results reveal biases from omitting country-specific financing conditions and highlight the need for climate finance across many sectors.

suggestions.title: Far-right political support and clean technology adoption in Germany
suggestions.authors: Sebastian Reining, Moritz Wussow, Chad Zanocco et al.
suggestions.abstract: The diffusion of clean technologies is critical for climate goals, yet political polarization influences adoption. Here we examine how ideology affects residential solar photovoltaic (PV) and electric vehicle (EV) uptake in Germany, drawing on responses from a three-wave individual-level survey, municipality-level observations of PV and EV registrations and election results. Supporters of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) show significantly lower willingness to adopt EVs and, to a lesser degree, PV systems compared with supporters of the pro-environmental Bündnis 90 / Die Grünen (GRÜNE) party. However, polarization is not static. The relative adoption gap between municipalities with strong AfD support and those with strong GRÜNE support declined from 76% to 31% for solar PV between 2000 and 2023, and from 84% to 60% for EVs between 2015 and 2019. Here, using an instrumental-variable strategy based on wolf attacks as a predictor of AfD vote share, we provide complementary evidence on the relationship between far-right voting and the adoption of clean technology. Counterfactual simulations indicate that, by 2023, solar PV diffusion could have been up to 1.3% higher and EV diffusion up to 2.9% higher in the absence of rising electoral support for the far right.

suggestions.title: Decoupling the cost estimations and equity implications of decarbonisation from carbon pricing
suggestions.authors: Shiya Zhao, Shinichiro Fujimori, Ken Oshiro, Tomoko Hasegawa
suggestions.abstract: Existing long-term climate mitigation scenarios typically rely on carbon pricing to estimate macroeconomic impacts and equity implications of decarbonisation, often projecting adverse distributional outcomes. However, substantial emissions reduction can also be achieved through non-carbon-pricing measures, raising concerns about the insights of these scenarios. Here, we decoupled the cost and equity assessment of decarbonisation from carbon pricing by developing decarbonisation scenarios independent of carbon pricing. We found that while the macroeconomic cost mainly comes from the system transition, the distributional effects indicated in conventional carbon-price-based scenarios are mainly caused by carbon prices, contributing to increases on poverty, hunger risks, and domestic income inequality by 86%, 84%, and 90%, respectively. Our findings indicate the great potential to moderate the concerns on the equity implications of climate change mitigation associated with carbon pricing and the need for improved policy representations in scenarios to better inform equitable and sustainable decarbonisation transitions.

suggestions.title: Spatially informed demand-side policies for green hydrogen diffusion in Europe
suggestions.authors: Christian Rumpelnik, Behnam Zakeri, Kavita Surana
suggestions.abstract: Green hydrogen faces an implementation gap: demand substantially lags policy ambitions. Here, combining an installation-level model of green hydrogen demand with an original database of >14,000 potential offtakers in Europe, we show that, conditional on diffusion patterns mirroring natural gas power generation (a historical analogue), demand-side spatial considerations are critical for closing this gap. Spatial spillovers—where local adoption increases adoption likelihood nearby—strongly shape diffusion, and their effect rises (>20-fold) when green hydrogen is not cost competitive. Spillover potential is concentrated in Central–Western Europe and hard-to-abate sectors: over half of the 10% most central installations are located in five German or Belgian industrial regions. Spatially informed policies deliver superior outcomes: targeting the most central offtakers improves policy cost-effectiveness by up to 41% (€0.96 kg −1 ) in a size, sector and cost-controlled setting and 15% (€0.20 kg −1 ) when following the European Hydrogen Bank auction format.

suggestions.title: Persistence of inequality in regional warming patterns under net-zero and overshoot pathways
suggestions.authors: Andrew King, Spencer Clark, Aditya Sengupta et al.
suggestions.abstract: As the world warms due to humanity’s continuing greenhouse gas emissions, almost every location across the planet is also warming significantly. Under net-zero or net-negative emissions pathways it is expected that global warming will greatly slow and global cooling may begin. However, relatively little is known about the pattern of post net-zero local temperature changes under these pathways compared with the warming pattern of today. Here, we explore the robustness of local temperature changes post net-zero using multiple modelling frameworks, and we investigate associated exposure and vulnerability. We find that a distinct pattern of Northern Hemisphere cooling and Southern Hemisphere warming can be found across temporal scales and model frameworks when examining local changes relative to global mean changes. By examining the signal-to-noise ratio of temperature changes we find that post net-zero warming or cooling is most detectable in tropical areas, not because the temperature changes there are largest but because interannual variability is small. The inequality seen in the pattern of present-day warming, where warming relative to background variability is higher in poorer tropical areas than in present-day wealthier high-latitude locations, will not reverse under net-zero emissions pathways and may take many decades to begin to reverse under net-negative emissions. suggestions.title: Assessing irrigation-driven carbon emissions across the Murray–Darling Basin: first insight from publicly available datasets
suggestions.authors: arezoo boroomandnia, Reihaneh Bandari, Behzad Rismanchi, Andrew Merchant
suggestions.abstract: Agricultural irrigation is the largest consumptive use of water in Australia. It heavily relies on energy-intensive pumping systems, linking water use to greenhouse gas emissions within the energy–water–food nexus. This study provides the first basin-scale estimate of irrigation energy use and associated emissions across the Murray–Darling Basin (MDB). It integrates publicly accessible datasets on agricultural energy, water use, and irrigation activity within a transparent and replicable top-down framework. Three scenarios were developed to estimate irrigation energy demand and associated emissions while reflecting uncertainty in irrigation’s share of agricultural energy use. Results indicate that irrigation-related emissions range from 4.5 to 9.01 Mt CO₂-e annually, corresponding to 0.53–1.06 t CO₂-e per ML of water applied. Emissions are dominated by grid electricity, although diesel use remains important in regions with limited grid access. Spatial analysis of proximity to electricity infrastructure enables a more refined allocation of energy sources. The results highlight spatial disparities in decarbonisation potential across the Basin. The findings demonstrate that electricity decarbonisation offers the greatest mitigation opportunity, complemented by electrification and decentralised renewable energy systems in off-grid areas. suggestions.title: Future Energy Transition Mineral Demands and Barriers for South and Southeast Asia
suggestions.authors: Seaver Wang, Peter Cook, Ryan Alimento et al.
suggestions.abstract: While the global geological availability of critical minerals is likely sufficient to support energy transition efforts, geographically imbalanced energy transition mineral production and consumption raise concerns around supply chain disruption and import dependence. While regions like Europe and the United States are actively studying such vulnerabilities, they remain relatively underexplored for emerging economies. This study uses a new, customizable mineral demand model for a wide set of commodities to estimate future energy transition mineral demand in the power generation and transport sectors for India, Bangladesh, and countries in ASEAN. Results indicate that ASEAN and South Asia may become significant consumers by 2050 on par with developed economies like the United States. In many cases, current mining in South and Southeast Asia falls short of projected regional demands. Both regions lack requisite graphite and lithium production. South Asia faces additional nickel, rare earths, copper, polysilicon, and cobalt deficits. Our results identify mineral supply-demand imbalances that may present future tradeoff risks between import dependence, downstream clean technology manufacturing ambitions, and public policy efforts to secure energy transition mineral supplies. Such results pose important implications particularly for countries like India, Vietnam, and Indonesia seeking to develop domestic solar, battery, and electric vehicle industries. suggestions.title: Emissions and system-level decarbonization pathways for global petrochemical production
suggestions.authors: Fanran Meng, Luke Cullen, Philip Mitchell et al.
suggestions.abstract: The petrochemical industry is responsible for 13% of global industrial and 3.5% of total greenhouse gas emissions, yet a globally consistent facility-level emissions inventory is lacking. Here we present a bottom-up assessment of historical, current and prospective emissions from 37,379 production facilities, covering 81 chemicals and 2,043 manufacturing processes. We estimate that petrochemical production emitted 2.0 ± 0.8 GtCO 2 e in 2023 and this could increase to 3.0 ± 1.2 GtCO 2 e by 2050 under a business-as-usual scenario. Emissions are highly concentrated, with 53% of 2023 emissions arising from 10% of facilities. Among primary chemicals, ethylene and ammonia were the largest emitters, at 290 ± 50 and 250 ± 50 MtCO 2 e, respectively, in 2023. Our scenario analysis indicates that decarbonization efforts should prioritize the highest-emitting facilities through efficiency improvements, alternative fuels and feedstocks, alongside broad demand reduction and power grid decarbonization. The analysis provides insights for industry, researchers and policymakers to target effective decarbonization in the petrochemical sector.
